readings.c1s1:
{{smaller block|Uncull’d, as came to hand. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 436.}}}}

¶
'''unculpable†''' (un-kul′pạ-bl), ''a.'' Inculpable.

'''uncult†''' (un-kult′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + *''cult'', < L. ''cultus'', pp. of ''colere'', cultivate: see ''cult'', ''n.'' Cf. ''incult.''] Uncultivated; rude; illiterate.

'''uncultivable''' (un-kul′ti-vạ-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being tilled or cultivated. ''Hawthorne'', Blithedale Romance, p. 155.

'''uncultivated''' (un-kul′ti-vā-ted), ''a.'' Not cultivated, in any sense of that word.

'''unculture†''' (un-kul′t̮ūr), ''n.'' Neglect or want of culture or education. ''Bp. Hall'', On Ps. cvii. 34.

'''uncumber†''', ''v.'' [ME. ''uncomberen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''cumber.''] To cease from encumbering.

'''uncumbered''' (un-kum′bėrd), ''a.'' Unencumbered. ''Dryden'', To John Driden, l. 18.

'''uncunning†''' (un-kun′ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''uncunning'', ''unkunnyng'', ''unconnynge'', ''unkonnynge'', ''onconninge''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''cunning'', ''n.''] Lack of knowledge or skill; ignorance. ''Chaucer.''

'''uncunning†''' (un-kun′ing), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unconnyng'', ''unkonnynge'', ''unconninde'', ''unconnand'', ''unkunand'', ''unconand''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''cunning'', ''a.''] Unknowing; ignorant; dull.
{{smaller block|Thise portours ben ''unkonnynge'' everemo.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 1139.}}}}

'''uncunningness†''' (un-kun′ing-nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unconnyngnesse''; < ''uncunning'', ''a.'', + ''-ness.''] Unknowingness; ignorance.
{{smaller block|<poem>O word For other myght take by lachesse,
Or perauenture by ''vnconnyngnesse.''</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 12.}}}}
readings.c1s3:
¶
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To lose its curl; come out of curl; become straight, as a lock of hair. ''Shak.'', Tit. And., ii. 3. 34.

'''uncurse†''' (un-kėrs′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''curse.''] To free from any execration; revoke a curse on. ''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 2. 137. [Rare.]

'''uncurtain''' (un-kėr′tạn), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''curtain.''] To remove or withdraw a curtain from; hence, to disclose; reveal; unveil.

'''uncus''' (ung′kus), ''n.''; pl. ''unci'' (un′sī). [NL., < L. ''uncus'', a hook, barb; cf. ''uncus'', hooked, curved. Hence ''unce''<sup>2</sup>, ''adunc'', ''aduncous'', etc.] '''1.''' The hook-like anterior extremity of the uncinate convolution of the brain.—'''2.''' In ''entom.'', the beak-like mesial prolongation of the eighth abdominal segment of lepidopterous insects. It forms no proper part of the organs ancillary to generation.—'''3.''' The head, hook, or comb of the malleolus or lateral tooth of the mastax of a wheel-animalcule.—'''4.''' In ''bot.'', a hook.

'''uncustomable''' (un-kus′tum-ạ-bl), ''a.'' Not subject to customs duties: as, ''uncustomable'' goods. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''uncustomed''' (un-kus′tumd), ''a.'' Not subjected to customs or duty; also, not having paid duty or been charged with customs; smuggled.
{{smaller block|One of them [Zacynthusians], at our being here, pursued a poor sailer for offering but to carry a little bag of Currans aboard ''uncustomed'', and killed him.
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes (1652), p. 6.}}
The buying or selling ''uncustomed'' goods.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXLIII. 282.}}}}
readings.c1s4:
¶
'''uncut''' (un-kut′), ''a.'' Not cut; specifically, in ''bookbinding,'' not trimmed across the bolts; having the full margin of the untrimmed sheets.
{{smaller block|If the bolts have been opened with a paper-knife without waste of margin, the book is said to be opened, but is ''uncut.''}}

'''undam''' (un-dam′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''dam''<sup>1</sup>.] To free from a dam, mound, or obstruction. [Rare.]

414
readings.c2s1:
{{smaller block|''Undams'' his watery stores.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Georgics, i. 157.}}}}

'''undashed''' (un-dasht′), ''a.'' Not dashed; not frightened or alarmed; undaunted.
{{smaller block|Yet stands he stiff, ''undashed'', unterrified.
{{right|''Daniel'', Civil Wars, vi.}}}}

'''undate''' (un′dāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''undatus'', pp. of ''undare'', rise in waves, < ''unda'', a wave: see ''ound'', ''undulate''.] '''1.''' Wavy; having a waved surface. ''Coues''.—'''2.''' In ''bot.'', same as ''undulate''.

'''undated<sup>1</sup>''' (un-dā′ted), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dated''.] Not dated; having no date: as, an ''undated'' letter or bill.

'''undated<sup>2</sup>''' (un′dā-ted), ''a.'' [< ''undate'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Having a waved surface; rising and falling in waves toward the margin, as a leaf; waved. Also ''undate''.—'''2.''' In ''her.'', same as ''undé''.—'''3.''' In ''bot.'', same as ''undulate''.

'''undaunted''' (un-dän′ted), ''a.'' Not daunted; not subdued or depressed by fear; bold; fearless; intrepid.
{{smaller block|<poem>By that Towr-tearing stroak I vnderstand
Th’ ''vndaunted'' strength of the Diuine right hand.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 2.}}
The Indian holds his course, silent, solitary, but ''undaunted'', through the boundless bosom of the wilderness.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 351.}}}}

'''undauntedly''' (un-dän′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an undaunted manner; boldly; intrepidly.
{{smaller block|A good conscience will make a man ''undauntedly'' confident.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, II. 176.}}}}

'''undauntedness''' (un-dän′ted-nes), ''n.'' Boldness; fearless bravery; intrepidity. ''Boyle''.

'''undawning''' (un-dâ′ning), ''a.'' Not yet dawning; not showing the dawn; not growing light.
readings.c2s2:
Thou [winter] hold’st the sun
A prisoner in the yet ''undawning'' east.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 130.}}</poem>}}
'''undé''' (un′dā), ''a.'' [< F. ''ondé'': see ''oundy''.] In ''her.'', wavy: noting a heraldic line such as separates two parts of the field, or a bearing from the field, and also of an ordinary, as a fesse or bend.
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|A Fesse Undé.}}}}

'''undeadliness†''' (un-ded′li-nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''undeedlinesse, undeadlinesse, undethlicnesse''; < ''undeadly'' + ''-ness''.] Incapability of dying; immortality.
{{smaller block|King of kyngis and Lord of lordis, . . . which aloone hath ''undeedlynesse''. {{right|''Wyclif'', 1 Tim. vi. 16.}}}}

'''undeadly†''' (un-ded′li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''undeedli, undedlic'', < AS. ''undeádlīc'' (= G. ''untötlich'' = Dan. ''udödelig''); as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''deadly'' (''deathly'').] Not subject to death; immortal. ''Wyclif'', 1 Tim. i. 17.

'''undeaf''' (un-def′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''deaf''.] To free from deafness; restore the sense of hearing to. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>My death’s sad tale may yet ''undeaf'' his ear.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 1. 16.}}</poem>}}

'''undeceivable''' (un-dẹ̄-sē′va̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not capable of being deceived; not subject to deception.
{{smaller block|This sure anchor of our ''undeceivable'' hope.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Letters concerning Falling away from Grace.}}}}
'''2.''' Incapable of deceiving; undeceitful. ''J. Hayward.''

'''undeceive''' (un-dē-sēv′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''deceive''.] To free from deception, cheat, fallacy, or mistake; open one’s eyes.
readings.c2s3:
¶
{{smaller block|This confirmed me in my opinion, and I was just going to leave him, when one of the natives . . . undertook to ''undeceive'' me.
{{right|''Cook'', Second Voyage, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Wounded, ''undeceived'', quivering with pain as he was, his heart still yearned after her.
{{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', Poor Gentleman, xlvii.}}}}

'''undecency†''' (un-dē′se̤n-si), ''n.'' Indecency. ''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Dying, iv. § 5.

'''undecennary''' (un-dē-sen′a̤-ri), ''a.'' [< L. ''undecim'', eleven (< ''unus'', one, + ''decem'', ten); after the analogy of ''decennary''<sup>1</sup>.] Eleventh; occurring once in every period of eleven years.

'''undecennial''' (un-dē-sen′i-al), ''a.'' [< L. ''undecim'', eleven; after the analogy of ''decennial''.] Belonging or relating to a period of eleven years; occurring or observed every eleven years, or every eleventh year: as, an ''undecennial'' festival.

'''undecent†''' (un-dē′se̤nt), ''a.'' Indecent; unsuitable; unbecoming.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fie, madam, how ''undecent'' ’tis for you,
So far unlike yourself, to be seen thus
In th’ open streets!</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Custom of the Country, iii. 5.}}}}

'''undecently†''' (un-dē′sent-li), ''adv.'' Indecently. ''Abp. Laud'', Hist. Church of Oxford, p. 61.

'''undecidable''' (un-dē-sī′da̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being decided, settled, or solved. [Rare.]
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|There is hardly a greater and more ''undecidable'' problem in natural theology. {{right|''South'', Sermons, III. vi.}}}}

'''undecide†''' (un-dẹ̄-sīd′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''decide.''] To reverse a decision concerning.
{{smaller block|To ''undecide'' the late concluded act they held for vain.
{{right|''Daniel'', Civil Wars, vii.}}}}

'''undecided''' (un-dẹ̄-sī′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not decided or determined; not settled.
{{smaller block|Long ''undecided'' lasts the airy strife.
{{right|''J. Philips'', Blenheim.}}}}
'''2.''' Not having one’s mind made up or one’s purpose fixed; irresolute.
{{smaller block|<poem>So doubted he, and, ''undecided'' yet,
Stood drawing forth his falchion huge.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Iliad, i.}}}}

'''undecidedly''' (un-dẹ̄-sī′ded-li), ''adv.'' In an undecided manner; irresolutely. ''H. Spencer'', Data of Ethics, p. 125.

'''undecimole''' (un-des′i-mōl), ''n.'' In ''music'', a group of eleven notes to be performed in the time of eight. Compare ''decimole'', ''triplet'', etc.

'''undecipherable''' (un-dẹ̄-sī′fėr-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Indecipherable. ''Chesterfield.''

'''undecisive''' (un-dẹ̄-sī′siv), ''a.'' Indecisive. ''Glanville.''

'''undeck''' (un-dek′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''deck''<sup>1</sup>.] To divest of ornaments or dress. ''Shak.'', Rich. II., iv. 1. 250.

'''undecked''' (un-dekt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not decked; not adorned.—'''2.''' Not having a deck: as, an ''undecked'' vessel or barge.

'''undeclinable''' (un-dẹ̄-klī′na̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' In ''gram.'', indeclinable.—'''2†.''' Not to be declined or avoided.
readings.c3s2:
¶
{{smaller block|I have shown how blameless the Lord Keeper was, and that the offence on his part was ''undeclinable''.
{{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, p. 107.}}}}

'''undeclined''' (un-dē-klīnd′), ''a.'' '''1†.''' Not deviating; not turned from the right way.
{{smaller block|His ''undeclined'' ways precisely kept.
{{right|''Sandys'', Paraphrase of Job.}}}}
'''2.''' Not having cases marked by different terminations: as, a noun ''undeclined''.

'''undecomposable''' (un-dē-kọm-pō′za̤-bl), ''a.'' Not admitting decomposition; that cannot be decomposed. ''H. Spencer.''

'''undeeded''' (un-dē′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not signalized by any great deed or action. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>My sword with an unbatter’d edge
I sheathe again, ''undeeded.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 7. 20.}}}}
'''2.''' Not transferred by deed: as, ''undeeded'' land.

'''undefaced''' (un-dē-fāst′), ''a.'' Not defaced; not deprived of its form; not disfigured.
{{smaller block|ffresshe, ''vndefacede'', & in fyne hew.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 8730.}}
He was his Maker’s image ''undefaced.'' {{right|''Coleridge.''}}}}

'''undefatigable†''' (un-dẹ̄-fat′i-ga̤-bl), ''a.'' Indefatigable.

'''undefeasible''' (un-dẹ̄-fē′zi-bl), ''a.'' Indefeasible. ''J. Udall'', On Luke xxii.

'''undefecated''' (un-def′ẹ̄-kā-ted), ''a.'' Not defecated; not cleared from dregs or impurities; unrefined; thick.
{{smaller block|Mine was pure, simple, ''undefecated'' rage.
{{right|''Godwin'', Mandeville, ii. 115. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unculpable†''' (un-kul′pạ-bl), ''a.'' Inculpable.

'''uncult†''' (un-kult′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + *''cult'', < L. ''cultus'', pp. of ''colere'', cultivate: see ''cult'', ''n.'' Cf. ''incult.''] Uncultivated; rude; illiterate.

'''uncultivable''' (un-kul′ti-vạ-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being tilled or cultivated. ''Hawthorne'', Blithedale Romance, p. 155.

'''uncultivated''' (un-kul′ti-vā-ted), ''a.'' Not cultivated, in any sense of that word.

'''unculture†''' (un-kul′t̮ūr), ''n.'' Neglect or want of culture or education. ''Bp. Hall'', On Ps. cvii. 34.

'''uncumber†''', ''v.'' [ME. ''uncomberen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''cumber.''] To cease from encumbering.

'''uncumbered''' (un-kum′bėrd), ''a.'' Unencumbered. ''Dryden'', To John Driden, l. 18.

'''uncunning†''' (un-kun′ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''uncunning'', ''unkunnyng'', ''unconnynge'', ''unkonnynge'', ''onconninge''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''cunning'', ''n.''] Lack of knowledge or skill; ignorance. ''Chaucer.''

'''uncunning†''' (un-kun′ing), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unconnyng'', ''unkonnynge'', ''unconninde'', ''unconnand'', ''unkunand'', ''unconand''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''cunning'', ''a.''] Unknowing; ignorant; dull.
{{smaller block|Thise portours ben ''unkonnynge'' everemo.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 1139.}}}}

'''uncunningness†''' (un-kun′ing-nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unconnyngnesse''; < ''uncunning'', ''a.'', + ''-ness.''] Unknowingness; ignorance.
{{smaller block|<poem>O word For other myght take by lachesse,
Or perauenture by ''vnconnyngnesse.''</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 12.}}}}

'''uncurable†''' (un-kūr′a-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uncurabil''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''curable''.] Incurable.
{{smaller block|An old man and a yong woman to content is ''vncurable.''
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 87.}}}}

'''uncurbable''' (un-kėr′ba-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being curbed or checked.
{{smaller block|So much ''uncurbable.''
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 2. 67.}}}}

'''uncurbed''' (un-kėrbd′), ''a.'' Not curbed, in any sense of that word.
{{smaller block|<poem>With frank and with ''uncurbed'' plainness
Tell us the Dauphin’s mind.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., i. 2. 244.}}}}

'''uncurious''' (un-kū′ri-us), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not curious or inquisitive; incurious; lacking curiosity.
{{smaller block|I would let my correspondents know that I have not been so ''uncurious'' a Spectator as not to have seen Prince Eugene.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 340.}}}}
'''2.''' Not curious, odd, or strange.
{{smaller block|He added very many particulars not ''uncurious'' concerning the manner of taking an audience.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 340.}}}}

'''uncurl''' (un-kėrl′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''curl''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To change from a curled condition or form; straighten out, as something which is curled.
{{smaller block|The lion ''uncurls'' his angry mane.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To lose its curl; come out of curl; become straight, as a lock of hair. ''Shak.'', Tit. And., ii. 3. 34.

'''uncurse†''' (un-kėrs′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''curse.''] To free from any execration; revoke a curse on. ''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 2. 137. [Rare.]

'''uncurtain''' (un-kėr′tạn), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''curtain.''] To remove or withdraw a curtain from; hence, to disclose; reveal; unveil.

'''uncus''' (ung′kus), ''n.''; pl. ''unci'' (un′sī). [NL., < L. ''uncus'', a hook, barb; cf. ''uncus'', hooked, curved. Hence ''unce''<sup>2</sup>, ''adunc'', ''aduncous'', etc.] '''1.''' The hook-like anterior extremity of the uncinate convolution of the brain.—'''2.''' In ''entom.'', the beak-like mesial prolongation of the eighth abdominal segment of lepidopterous insects. It forms no proper part of the organs ancillary to generation.—'''3.''' The head, hook, or comb of the malleolus or lateral tooth of the mastax of a wheel-animalcule.—'''4.''' In ''bot.'', a hook.

'''uncustomable''' (un-kus′tum-ạ-bl), ''a.'' Not subject to customs duties: as, ''uncustomable'' goods. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''uncustomed''' (un-kus′tumd), ''a.'' Not subjected to customs or duty; also, not having paid duty or been charged with customs; smuggled.
{{smaller block|One of them [Zacynthusians], at our being here, pursued a poor sailer for offering but to carry a little bag of Currans aboard ''uncustomed'', and killed him.
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes (1652), p. 6.}}
The buying or selling ''uncustomed'' goods.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXLIII. 282.}}}}

'''uncut''' (un-kut′), ''a.'' Not cut; specifically, in ''bookbinding,'' not trimmed across the bolts; having the full margin of the untrimmed sheets.
{{smaller block|If the bolts have been opened with a paper-knife without waste of margin, the book is said to be opened, but is ''uncut.''}}

'''undam''' (un-dam′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''dam''<sup>1</sup>.] To free from a dam, mound, or obstruction. [Rare.]

414 {{smaller block|''Undams'' his watery stores.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Georgics, i. 157.}}}}

'''undashed''' (un-dasht′), ''a.'' Not dashed; not frightened or alarmed; undaunted.
{{smaller block|Yet stands he stiff, ''undashed'', unterrified.
{{right|''Daniel'', Civil Wars, vi.}}}}

'''undate''' (un′dāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''undatus'', pp. of ''undare'', rise in waves, < ''unda'', a wave: see ''ound'', ''undulate''.] '''1.''' Wavy; having a waved surface. ''Coues''.—'''2.''' In ''bot.'', same as ''undulate''.

'''undated<sup>1</sup>''' (un-dā′ted), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dated''.] Not dated; having no date: as, an ''undated'' letter or bill.

'''undated<sup>2</sup>''' (un′dā-ted), ''a.'' [< ''undate'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Having a waved surface; rising and falling in waves toward the margin, as a leaf; waved. Also ''undate''.—'''2.''' In ''her.'', same as ''undé''.—'''3.''' In ''bot.'', same as ''undulate''.

'''undaunted''' (un-dän′ted), ''a.'' Not daunted; not subdued or depressed by fear; bold; fearless; intrepid.
{{smaller block|<poem>By that Towr-tearing stroak I vnderstand
Th’ ''vndaunted'' strength of the Diuine right hand.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 2.}}
The Indian holds his course, silent, solitary, but ''undaunted'', through the boundless bosom of the wilderness.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 351.}}}}

'''undauntedly''' (un-dän′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an undaunted manner; boldly; intrepidly.
{{smaller block|A good conscience will make a man ''undauntedly'' confident.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, II. 176.}}}}

'''undauntedness''' (un-dän′ted-nes), ''n.'' Boldness; fearless bravery; intrepidity. ''Boyle''.

'''undawning''' (un-dâ′ning), ''a.'' Not yet dawning; not showing the dawn; not growing light. Thou [winter] hold’st the sun
A prisoner in the yet ''undawning'' east.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 130.}}</poem>}}
'''undé''' (un′dā), ''a.'' [< F. ''ondé'': see ''oundy''.] In ''her.'', wavy: noting a heraldic line such as separates two parts of the field, or a bearing from the field, and also of an ordinary, as a fesse or bend. {{img float|file=century v08 p0397 c2f1.png|width=88px|align=right|cap={{smaller|A Fesse Undé.}}}}

'''undeadliness†''' (un-ded′li-nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''undeedlinesse, undeadlinesse, undethlicnesse''; < ''undeadly'' + ''-ness''.] Incapability of dying; immortality.
{{smaller block|King of kyngis and Lord of lordis, . . . which aloone hath ''undeedlynesse''. {{right|''Wyclif'', 1 Tim. vi. 16.}}}}

'''undeadly†''' (un-ded′li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''undeedli, undedlic'', < AS. ''undeádlīc'' (= G. ''untötlich'' = Dan. ''udödelig''); as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''deadly'' (''deathly'').] Not subject to death; immortal. ''Wyclif'', 1 Tim. i. 17.

'''undeaf''' (un-def′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''deaf''.] To free from deafness; restore the sense of hearing to. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>My death’s sad tale may yet ''undeaf'' his ear.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 1. 16.}}</poem>}}

'''undeceivable''' (un-dẹ̄-sē′va̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not capable of being deceived; not subject to deception.
{{smaller block|This sure anchor of our ''undeceivable'' hope.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Letters concerning Falling away from Grace.}}}}
'''2.''' Incapable of deceiving; undeceitful. ''J. Hayward.''

'''undeceive''' (un-dē-sēv′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''deceive''.] To free from deception, cheat, fallacy, or mistake; open one’s eyes.

{{smaller block|This confirmed me in my opinion, and I was just going to leave him, when one of the natives . . . undertook to ''undeceive'' me.
{{right|''Cook'', Second Voyage, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Wounded, ''undeceived'', quivering with pain as he was, his heart still yearned after her.
{{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', Poor Gentleman, xlvii.}}}}

'''undecency†''' (un-dē′se̤n-si), ''n.'' Indecency. ''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Dying, iv. § 5.

'''undecennary''' (un-dē-sen′a̤-ri), ''a.'' [< L. ''undecim'', eleven (< ''unus'', one, + ''decem'', ten); after the analogy of ''decennary''<sup>1</sup>.] Eleventh; occurring once in every period of eleven years.

'''undecennial''' (un-dē-sen′i-al), ''a.'' [< L. ''undecim'', eleven; after the analogy of ''decennial''.] Belonging or relating to a period of eleven years; occurring or observed every eleven years, or every eleventh year: as, an ''undecennial'' festival.

'''undecent†''' (un-dē′se̤nt), ''a.'' Indecent; unsuitable; unbecoming.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fie, madam, how ''undecent'' ’tis for you,
So far unlike yourself, to be seen thus
In th’ open streets!</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Custom of the Country, iii. 5.}}}}

'''undecently†''' (un-dē′sent-li), ''adv.'' Indecently. ''Abp. Laud'', Hist. Church of Oxford, p. 61.

'''undecidable''' (un-dē-sī′da̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being decided, settled, or solved. [Rare.] {{smaller block|There is hardly a greater and more ''undecidable'' problem in natural theology. {{right|''South'', Sermons, III. vi.}}}}

'''undecide†''' (un-dẹ̄-sīd′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''decide.''] To reverse a decision concerning.
{{smaller block|To ''undecide'' the late concluded act they held for vain.
{{right|''Daniel'', Civil Wars, vii.}}}}

'''undecided''' (un-dẹ̄-sī′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not decided or determined; not settled.
{{smaller block|Long ''undecided'' lasts the airy strife.
{{right|''J. Philips'', Blenheim.}}}}
'''2.''' Not having one’s mind made up or one’s purpose fixed; irresolute.
{{smaller block|<poem>So doubted he, and, ''undecided'' yet,
Stood drawing forth his falchion huge.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Iliad, i.}}}}

'''undecidedly''' (un-dẹ̄-sī′ded-li), ''adv.'' In an undecided manner; irresolutely. ''H. Spencer'', Data of Ethics, p. 125.

'''undecimole''' (un-des′i-mōl), ''n.'' In ''music'', a group of eleven notes to be performed in the time of eight. Compare ''decimole'', ''triplet'', etc.

'''undecipherable''' (un-dẹ̄-sī′fėr-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Indecipherable. ''Chesterfield.''

'''undecisive''' (un-dẹ̄-sī′siv), ''a.'' Indecisive. ''Glanville.''

'''undeck''' (un-dek′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''deck''<sup>1</sup>.] To divest of ornaments or dress. ''Shak.'', Rich. II., iv. 1. 250.

'''undecked''' (un-dekt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not decked; not adorned.—'''2.''' Not having a deck: as, an ''undecked'' vessel or barge.

'''undeclinable''' (un-dẹ̄-klī′na̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' In ''gram.'', indeclinable.—'''2†.''' Not to be declined or avoided.

{{smaller block|I have shown how blameless the Lord Keeper was, and that the offence on his part was ''undeclinable''.
{{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, p. 107.}}}}

'''undeclined''' (un-dē-klīnd′), ''a.'' '''1†.''' Not deviating; not turned from the right way.
{{smaller block|His ''undeclined'' ways precisely kept.
{{right|''Sandys'', Paraphrase of Job.}}}}
'''2.''' Not having cases marked by different terminations: as, a noun ''undeclined''.

'''undecomposable''' (un-dē-kọm-pō′za̤-bl), ''a.'' Not admitting decomposition; that cannot be decomposed. ''H. Spencer.''

'''undeeded''' (un-dē′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not signalized by any great deed or action. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>My sword with an unbatter’d edge
I sheathe again, ''undeeded.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 7. 20.}}}}
'''2.''' Not transferred by deed: as, ''undeeded'' land.

'''undefaced''' (un-dē-fāst′), ''a.'' Not defaced; not deprived of its form; not disfigured.
{{smaller block|ffresshe, ''vndefacede'', & in fyne hew.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 8730.}}
He was his Maker’s image ''undefaced.'' {{right|''Coleridge.''}}}}

'''undefatigable†''' (un-dẹ̄-fat′i-ga̤-bl), ''a.'' Indefatigable.

'''undefeasible''' (un-dẹ̄-fē′zi-bl), ''a.'' Indefeasible. ''J. Udall'', On Luke xxii.

'''undefecated''' (un-def′ẹ̄-kā-ted), ''a.'' Not defecated; not cleared from dregs or impurities; unrefined; thick.
{{smaller block|Mine was pure, simple, ''undefecated'' rage.
{{right|''Godwin'', Mandeville, ii. 115. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''undefiled''' (un-dẹ̄-fīld′), ''a.'' Not made unclean or impure; unsullied; uncorrupted; unpolluted; unimpaired; immaculate; innocent. Ps. cix. 1.

'''undefinable''' (un-dẹ̄-fī′na-bl), ''a.'' Not definable, in any sense; indefinable: as, the ''undefinable'' bounds of space.

{{smaller block|Why simple ideas are ''undefinable'' is that, the several terms of a definition signifying several ideas, they can all by no means represent an idea which has no composition at all. {{right|''Locke'', Human Understanding, iii. 4.}}}}

'''undefine''' (un-dẹ̄-fīn′), ''v. i.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''define.''] To render something indefinite; confound or confuse definitions. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|In fact, their application to logic, or any other subject, is hereafter only to ''undefine'' and to confuse. {{right|''Sir W. Hamilton.''}}}}

'''undefined''' (un-dẹ̄-fīnd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not defined or explained; not described by definition or explanation.

{{smaller block|Obscure, doubtful, ''undefined'' words. {{right|''Locke.''}}}}

'''2.''' Not having limits distinctly marked or seen; not definitely limited; indefinite.

{{smaller block|An ''undefined'', undefinable, ideal responsibility to the public judgement. {{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Senate, May 7, 1834.}}

''Undefined'' and undefinable rights. {{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 107.}}}}

'''undefouled†''' (un-dẹ̄-fould′), ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''defouled.''] Undefiled; immaculate.

{{smaller block|Moder of God, and Virgin ''undefouled.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Mother of God, l. 1.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
